extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students and early-career mathematicians (undergraduates, graduate students, postdocs, junior faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, stage-by-stage guidance for pursuing an academic career in mathematics, covering undergraduate, graduate, postdoc and early-career issues (time management, research practice, presentations, skills, advisor relations, and career choices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work hard
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to work hard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a fundamental expectation at the graduate level; paired with working professionally and enjoying your work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work professionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Work professionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasised alongside hard work; implies maintaining professional standards in research, communication, and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enjoy your work
rubrics_metrics.description: But it is also important to enjoy your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice not to sacrifice personal satisfaction — enjoyment is presented as an important complement to effort and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think ahead
rubrics_metrics.description: Think ahead to understand the way forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan research and career steps proactively rather than reacting; helps orient choices and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask yourself dumb questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask yourself dumb questions to understand the way before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple/basic questions to clarify understanding and reveal hidden assumptions before proceeding on a project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend talks and conferences, even those not directly related to your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to different areas can spark ideas, broaden perspective, and build networks; recommended at graduate and postdoc stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talk to your advisor and take initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to your advisor, but also take the initiative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult your advisor for guidance while proactively proposing directions, problems, and steps; balance dependence and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature obsession with one big problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t prematurely obsess on a single “big problem” or “big theory”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversify projects and avoid locking into one long-shot project too early in your career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write down and make your work available
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down what you’ve done, and make your work available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep records, write papers/notes, and disseminate results (preprints, talks) so your work is visible and usable by others; see linked advice on how to write and submit papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continually relearn and learn outside your field
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn and relearn your field, but don’t be afraid to learn things outside your field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain depth by revisiting fundamentals while gaining breadth by studying other areas that may provide new tools or perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know limits and strengths of tools; aim beyond current range
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn the limitations of your tools, but also learn the power of other mathematician’s tools. In particular, you should continually aim just beyond your current range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about what your current techniques can/can't do, learn others' methods, and push slightly beyond comfort to grow capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be flexible and patient in research
rubrics_metrics.description: In your research, be both flexible and patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt to new information and be willing to change directions; accept that progress can be slow and requires persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and present research; tailor talks to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You should definitely travel and present your research if given the opportunity. But be considerate of your audience; talks are not the same as papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek opportunities to present (conferences, seminars) while preparing presentations differently from written papers (audience, exposition, scope).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical of your own work; discard when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Be sceptical of your own work, and don’t be afraid to use the wastebasket.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate and, if necessary, abandon or rework directions that are unproductive; treat drafts and ideas as disposable resources during exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time management
rubrics_metrics.description: My thoughts on time management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time management is flagged as an important meta-skill; the author links to more detailed notes on organizing time and maintaining productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame; study at different places
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t base career decisions on glamour or fame. But you should study at different places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose programs for substantive training and fit rather than reputation alone; gaining experience at different institutions is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Programming skills: useful but field-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming is a useful general skill to have, but I think in most areas of pure mathematics it is not necessary (beyond the rudimentary level...). In the more numerical parts of applied mathematics programming skills are of course somewhat more essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop programming skills appropriate to your subfield: basic computational tools for pure math, more advanced programming for numerical/applied areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value breadth beyond grades and formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that there is more to maths than grades and exams and methods; there is also more to maths than rigour and proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise conceptual understanding, problem-solving experience, creativity and other non-graded skills alongside formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss major career decisions with your advisor
rubrics_metrics.description: I would in particular recommend discussing such decisions with your advisor if you have one, as he or she will be familiar with your situation and will likely be able to provide pertinent advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your advisor’s local knowledge of opportunities and constraints when making choices about projects, programs, or career moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: If stuck on thesis research, seek alternate projects with advisor
rubrics_metrics.description: I would recommend that you talk to your thesis advisor on possible alternate projects, either related to your existing project or quite different in nature; I assume in the last three years that you have acquired enough background in your chosen areas of mathematics that you should be aware of other work that is going on and the type of problems to which the tools you have learned may be applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a project stalls, proactively consult the advisor about pivoting, applying learned tools to new problems, or finding a different direction for the thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn proofs by active reconstruction and teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the best ways to memorise the proof of X is to cover up the proof and try to prove it yourself... The very best ways to learn the proof of X, of course, are to teach about it in a class, or to adapt that proof for one’s own research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice proofs by attempting them unaided, revealing key 'tricks' when stuck, teaching material, and adapting proofs in research to internalize methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undergraduate preparation for graduate admissions (non-math majors)
rubrics_metrics.description: First thing is to study some linear algebra and little bit of analysis and maybe some abstract algebra the basic stuff ... then you can write some exams ... tifr and imsc also have summer research opportunities ... if you want to study in U.S. i think you have to take the gre math exam and take several courses in undergraduate math.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For students from other majors: take core math courses (linear algebra, analysis, abstract algebra), pursue summer research, and satisfy admissions/testing (GRE math) requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: For research careers prefer strong training and connections
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to work in a flashy area it is most important to work directly under the leader in that area ... You should go to the best place you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a top program or working with leading researchers helps you avoid wasted effort on already-resolved or rapidly moving problems; this is advice from commenters that the author republishes as part of the discussion.
